Q: What is the technical description/meaning of the term 'snapshot' (regarding Git)? A:

It is true that every commit stores a snapshot of the project, just like a backup of the files at a particular point in time.

But talking about "changes made by a commit" is misleading, because a commit does not make or store changes. (Remember, it stores the whole project state.) Changes only come into play when a commit is compared to another commit.

Of course, Git isn't as silly as to make a whole copy of the entire project for every commit. But the cleverness employed to optimize storage is just an implementation detail. The higher-level point of view must be that a Git commit stores the whole project state (a "snapshot").

Q: Which exception to throw for invalid input which is valid from client perspective A:

The question is is throwing illegal argument exception the right thing to do?

There is no single "right thing to do". It depends on how you want / need to "frame" this condition; i.e. is it a bug, a user input error, or something that the program is supposed to be able to deal with?

  • If the case of two lines not intersecting is unequivocally a "bug", then IllegalArgumentException is fine. This is what the exception is designed for. (Note that it is an unchecked exception, so the expectation is that it won't be caught / recovered from.)

  • If this is a case that you expect the program to be able to recover from by itself, then a custom exception is the best idea. That way, you reduce the possibility of your code getting confused by (say) a library method throwing (say) an IllegalArgumentException ... than means something other than "two lines intersected".

  • If this case is something that you expect to report to the end user as part of input validation, then a generic "validation error" exception might be more appropriate than a specific custom exception. However, this method doesn't look like it is designed to be used (solely) for user input validation.

In some contexts, it may be objectively better1 to not throw an exception at all, but (IMO) this is not one of those contexts.

The alternatives to throwing an exception are returning null or an Optional<Point> or returning a Point value that means "no such point" to the calling code. The problems with these alternatives are:

  • If you return null or an "empty" Optional the caller has to explicitly and correctly deal with the null or "empty" case ... or this will lead to NPEs or NoSuchElement exceptions.
  • There is no natural Point instance that could be used to mean "not a point"2.

This is not to say that you couldn't make these alternatives work. It is just that in this context, it will probably be more work to do that, and probably there won't be a tangible pay-off.

1 - I am excluding dogmatic reasons ... like "exceptions should only be used for exceptional events".
2 - I am assuming Point is java.awt.Point or similar. Obviously you could define and use a custom Point class which provides a "no such point" instance. But it will come at a cost. And you will need to deal with the case where code accidentally uses the "no such point" instance in some computation. And you are probably back where you started; i.e. throwing an exception!

Q: Is switching from C++ to Python for DSA a good decision? A:

App devs don't need to care about how a library (including AIs or MLs) are implemented, they only need to know how it's used, the weakness and strength. So strictly speaking it doesn't matter if a dev using, say, EmbeddingGemma know how to train an LLM, as long as they know the basics about token context. It's the same way app devs only need to know a dictionary can retrieve arbitrary record much faster than a list as long as they can define a relatively unique key.

Library devs are different matters, but usually for regular apps you'd already have a decent framework to work with.

Q: How to handle an undefined connection from accept() in HTTP::Daemon:SSL? A:

The strace shows that the TCP accept call succeeded. It is also followed by the read and write on the socket, which look like the TLS handshake. It looks though that the TLS handshake was not successfully completed, based on the length the last read from the client looks like an encrypted TLS alert. Since it is encrypted one can only guess the content though.

My guess is that the client can not successfully validate the servers certificate. In this case the alert might be something like "unknown ca". TLS errors are not reflected in $! but in $IO::Socket::SSL::SSL_ERROR, so check there for details. It can also help to run your code with perl -MIO::Socket::SSL=debug9 to enable most verbose TLS debugging.

Apart from that accept can not only fail with EINTR but also with ECONNABORTED, i.e. when the client closed the connection already after a successful TCP handshake but before accept returned. Since this is a recoverable problem (just wait for the next accept) better check for this error too instead of exiting the loop.
